content: Sweet Flag, also known as Calamus or Common Sweet Flag (Acorus calamus), is a perennial wetland plant belonging to the Acoraceae family and the Acorus genus. It is characterized by its tall stature, aromatic leaves, and rhizomes, which have been historically utilized for medicinal purposes, their fragrance, and as a psychotropic agent. The plant is referred to by various names, including cinnamon sedge, flagroot, gladdon, myrtle flag, myrtle grass, myrtle sedge, sweet cane, sweet myrtle, sweet root, sweet rush, and sweet sedge. While it is likely native to India, Acorus calamus is now distributed across Europe, southern Russia, northern Asia Minor, southern Siberia, China, Japan, Burma, Sri Lanka, and northern regions of the United States. Botanical Characteristics The differentiation between Acorus species is based on the number and prominence of leaf veins. Acorus calamus is distinguished by a single prominent midvein, flanked by slightly raised secondary veins that are less than half the diameter of the midvein, along with numerous fine tertiary veins. This feature sets it apart from Acorus americanus. The leaves of Acorus calamus range in width from 0.7 to 1.7 cm, with an average width of approximately 1 cm. The sympodial leaf is slightly shorter than the vegetative leaves, and the leaf margins are wavy or undulate. The spadix, which is the flowering structure, can grow to a length of 4.9 to 8.9 cm during its expansion phase, making it longer than that of Acorus americanus. The flowers of Acorus calamus are also longer, measuring between 3 and 4 mm. Notably, Acorus calamus is infertile, as evidenced by its abortive ovary, which appears shriveled. Chemical Composition The chemical profile of Acorus calamus varies depending on its ploidy. Both triploid and tetraploid varieties of the plant contain asarone, a compound with psychoactive properties. However, the diploid variety does not produce asarone. Regulatory Status In 1968, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) banned the use of calamus and its derivatives, such as calamus oil, as food additives and medicinal products due to safety concerns. Historical and Medicinal Uses Acorus calamus has been a traded commodity in various cultures for thousands of years and has been employed medicinally to address a wide range of ailments. In ancient times, particularly in the Orient and Egypt, the rhizome was believed to possess aphrodisiac properties. In Europe, the plant was often added to wine, and its root is considered one of the potential ingredients in absinthe. Among northern Native American tribes, Acorus calamus has been used both as a medicinal agent and as a stimulant. Additionally, the root is thought to have been employed as an entheogen, a substance used to induce spiritual or hallucinogenic experiences, by some northern Native American groups. At high doses, the plant exhibits hallucinogenic effects. Cultural Symbolism The calamus plant has long been associated with male love and affection. Its name is linked to a Greek myth involving Kalamos, the son of the river god Maeander, who loved Karpos, the son of Zephyrus and Chloris. When Karpos drowned, Kalamos was transformed into a reed, whose rustling in the wind was interpreted as a lamentation. The plant was a favorite of Henry David Thoreau, who referred to it as sweet flag, and of Walt Whitman, who included a section titled The Calamus Poems in the third edition of his work Leaves of Grass (1860). In these poems, the calamus serves as a symbol of love, desire, and affection. Some interpretations suggest that this symbolism arises from the visual resemblance of the spadix to an erect human penis. The name Sweet Flag is derived from the plant's sweet fragrance and the wavy edges of its leaves, which are thought to resemble a fluttering flag. In Japan, the plant symbolizes the bravery of samurai warriors due to its sharp, sword-like leaves. Even today, during the Boy's Festival (Tango no Sekku) on May 5, many Japanese families with young boys partake in a Sweet Flag Bath (shōbu yu) as part of the celebration. Etymology of the Word Calamus The term calamus originates from Latin and has cognates in Greek (kalamos, meaning reed) and Sanskrit (kalama, meaning reed, pen, and a type of rice). This linguistic connection suggests that the word predates these languages and likely originates from their common ancestor, Proto-Indo-European. The Arabic word qalam (meaning pen) is believed to have been borrowed from one of these languages or directly from Indo-European. Several modern English words are derived from the Latin root calamus: Calamari, meaning squid, originates from the Latin calamarium, which refers to an ink horn or pen case, as reeds were historically used as writing tools. Calumet, another term for the Native American peace pipe, which was often crafted from hollow reeds. Shawm, a medieval woodwind instrument similar to an oboe, which produces sound through a vibrating reed mouthpiece. Chalumeau register, referring to the lower range of notes on a clarinet, another reed-based instrument.
